stops.title: Burning buried sunshine
stops.blurb: Before industry, almost all the energy people used for heat and work came from each year's plant growth, which set a hard limit on what an economy could make. In England people turned to coal: the energy of plants, stored over geological ages. Energy use rose massively, and output with it. Worldwide, burning it released about 9 million tonnes of carbon dioxide in 1750, and 3.5 billion in 1913.

stops.title: Declarations of rights
stops.blurb: On 4 July 1776, thirteen British colonies in North America declared their independence, holding it "self-evident, that all men are created equal" and that governments get their powers from "the consent of the governed". In August 1789, France's National Assembly declared that "men are born and remain free and equal in rights". Both set out the idea that government exists to protect the rights of the people.

stops.title: Haiti: freedom won by the enslaved
stops.blurb: In 1791, in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved Africans rose up in the first and only successful revolt of its kind. Their leader, Toussaint Louverture, controlled the colony by 1801, but Napoleon had him arrested; he died in a French prison in 1803. In 1804 the French surrendered and Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared independence. Haiti became the first independent Black republic.

stops.title: Vaccines and germs
stops.blurb: In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner inoculated an 8-year-old boy with matter from a dairymaid's cowpox sores, then with smallpox; the boy did not fall ill. Jenner named the method vaccination, from vacca, Latin for cow. In 1854 John Snow linked a London cholera outbreak to a single water pump, and in 1876 Robert Koch identified the bacterium that causes anthrax.

stops.title: The first billion people
stops.blurb: For almost all of history the number of people grew very slowly. By the best estimates, the world passed one billion people for the first time around 1805. In 1750 there had been about 750 million; by 1914 there were about 1.8 billion. The second billion took little more than a century, where the first had taken the whole of human history.
stops.dateNote: Population figures before 1950 are estimates; the year the world passed one billion is uncertain by several years.

p: Smallpox was one of the deadliest diseases in history. In 18th-century Europe it killed about 400,000 people a year, and a third of those who survived went blind. People had long practised variolation: infecting a healthy person on purpose with matter from a smallpox sore, so that they caught a milder case and were protected afterwards. The method reached Europe from Istanbul early in the 1700s. In England it was championed by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had her son inoculated in 1718. It was risky: 2 to 3 percent of variolated people died.

In May 1796 Edward Jenner took matter from the cowpox sores on the hand of a dairymaid, Sarah Nelms, and inoculated an 8-year-old boy, James Phipps. In July he inoculated the boy again, this time with matter from a fresh smallpox sore. No disease developed. Jenner published his cases in 1798 and called the method vaccination, from *vacca*, Latin for cow.
Jenner set out his experiment in a booklet, *An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae*, after the Royal Society rejected a short report on it in 1797.

Half a century later, most doctors still believed that diseases spread through "bad air", the miasma theory. During a cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London in 1854, John Snow argued that cholera spread through water. He compared the water sources of people who fell ill and found a clear link with one public pump, and its handle was removed. In 1876 Robert Koch identified the bacterium that causes anthrax, which launched medical bacteriology and a "golden age" of discoveries.

Jenner did not start from nothing. For years he had heard that dairymaids who caught cowpox were protected from smallpox. Parts of his explanation were wrong: his idea that cowpox began as a disease of horses was discredited in his own lifetime. His *Inquiry* met a mixed reaction from doctors, and when he went to London to find volunteers, he found none for three months.

Later science, including the germ theory of disease and the study of viruses, largely bore out Jenner's main conclusions. Vaccination made it possible to wipe out smallpox altogether. On 8 May 1980 the World Health Assembly announced that the world was free of it.
